landmark_cases.title: Niang v. Gonzales
landmark_cases.reason: Sets out the core asylum framework in the Tenth Circuit: statutory definition of “refugee” and the three required elements for past persecution, including the government unable-or-unwilling prong.

landmark_cases.title: Rivera-Barrientos v. Holder
landmark_cases.reason: Foundational on the nexus requirement, articulating the “one central reason” standard and mixed-motive analysis for persecution on account of a protected ground.

landmark_cases.title: Wiransane v. Ashcroft
landmark_cases.reason: Defines persecution in the Tenth Circuit as harm beyond mere restrictions or threats, a key threshold concept applied to evaluate whether alleged mistreatment rises to persecution.

landmark_cases.title: Karki v. Holder
landmark_cases.reason: Clarifies that threats alone generally do not constitute persecution while physical injury is not strictly required—guidance central to assessing cumulative harm claims.

landmark_cases.title: Singh v. Bondi
landmark_cases.reason: Recent Tenth Circuit guidance on the government “unable or unwilling” standard, emphasizing reporting/notice to authorities and the futility-or-danger exception.

landmark_cases.title: Dallakoti v. Holder
landmark_cases.reason: Reinforces that a protected ground cannot be incidental or tangential; it must be at least one central reason for the harm—key to the political-opinion nexus analysis.
